_meta.directives: Fiche approfondie selon le protocole de recherche anthroponymique ; chaque affirmation positive renvoie à une source dédiée et les absences sont déclarées dans gaps.

oralTraditions.claim: Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré are said to be the children of one and the same Fula mother. In this narrative, Diakité was the chief and Sangaré the scholar.
oralTraditions.carrier: Babou Condé, griot du village de Fadama, dans la préfecture de Kouroussa en Guinée
oralTraditions.collector: E. A. Bogacheva, lors d'entretiens menés en 2017
oralTraditions.context: Narrative reported in Russian in a university thesis

oralTraditions.claim: Wassoulou is said to have been founded by Fula from Fouta-Djalon, led by Kali Diallo and assisted by his brother Pathé Diallo.
oralTraditions.collector: Aly Gilbert Iffono, historien guinéen, dans son Lexique historique de la Guinée-Conakry
oralTraditions.context: Oral tradition reported in French, known here through a 2024 online article that summarises it; Iffono's book was not read directly

writtenChronicles.claim: A work written in N'ko by Souleymane Kanté traces Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré back to a single group that he calls jàtará, itself descended from the Fula. The name is transcribed Sánkare in the translation.

historicalSyntheses.claim: One explanation links the presence of the name among Malinke lineages to borrowing: Malinke clans subjugated by the Fulani are said to have taken the names of their masters, Sangaré, Diallo, Sidibé and Diakité. This explanation is reported only by an online press article.

The Fulani of Wassoulou traditionally identify themselves by four names: Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré. They no longer speak Fulani today; several competing reasons are given, either marriages with local women, who spoke their own language to the children, or the ban on Fulani imposed by the conqueror Samori Touré.

In Guinea, a Guinean consultant describes the bearers of the name as originating from Wassoulou, Fulani integrated into the Malinke through language and customs; they are classed sometimes among one, sometimes among the other.

In Mali, Sangaré is counted among the Fulani family names, including among the Foula of Wassoulou, in the regions of Koulikoro, Kita, Bafoulabé and Sikasso, who claim membership of the great Fulani family although they no longer speak the language.

Among the Fulani of western Burkina Faso, Sangaré is given as one of the four main Fulani clans, with Diallo, Diakité and Sidibé. Sidibé and Sangaré form there one of the two pairs at the mythical core of Fulani identity, in a relation of equivalence, and the two names are linked by a joking relationship.
Among the Fulani of western Burkina Faso, the Bingaabe are usually classed in the Sangaré clan; they are joking allies of the Toroobe.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary consulted gives a meaning for the word. The dictionary of Manding clan names writes it Sàngare, with the variant Sankare, links it to the Fula, to Wassoulou and to the Malinké, and gives Bari, Si and Ba as its equivalents. It also records a joking nickname, Kàngare.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: No source consulted links the name to a caste status or a hereditary occupation. The society of Wassoulou, predominantly Fula, is described as never having adopted the caste system of its Mandinka neighbours: there are no griots there.

homonyms.label: Sangare (Inde)
homonyms.distinction: The same spelling is borne in India, where an aggregator counts about 5,400 bearers and transcribes it in Marathi. No source consulted links it to the West African family name; it is noted so that the two are not confused.

sources.title: New Tools for the Analysis of Political Power in Africa
sources.notes: Ilia Rainer and Francesco Trebbi, NBER Working Paper 18424, September 2012. The appendix on Guinea, p. 42, separately explains the classification of Diakite, Sidibe and Sangare: originating from Wassoulou, described as Fula integrated into the Malinké populations, they are coded by the authors as half Fula and half Malinké. The paper states that it has not been peer-reviewed.

sources.title: Histoire du Wassoulou : ce qu'il faut retenir
sources.notes: Article by Justin Morel, published online on 7 May 2024, not peer-reviewed. It presents the founding of Wassoulou by Kali and Pathé Diallo as an oral tradition reported by the Guinean historian Aly Gilbert Iffono (Lexique historique de la Guinée-Conakry, L'Harmattan, 1992). The four names of the Fula of Wassoulou, the reasons for the loss of Fula and the adoption of these names by Malinké clans are given by the article itself, and it cannot be said whether they come from Iffono. Iffono's work has not been read directly.

sources.title: Oumou Sangaré : malienne, femme et artiste
sources.notes: François Bensignor, Hommes & Migrations, no. 1206, March–April 1997, pp. 137–139 (Persée). Places Wassoulou, predominantly Fula, in southern Mali, near the borders with Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso, and writes that its inhabitants have never adopted the caste system of the Mandinka peoples (absence of griots).

sources.title: Sangare — origine, signification et répartition du nom
sources.notes: Aggregator site for family-name statistics, with no verifiable independent editorial review; 2014 data, consulted in an archived copy from 2024. It counts about 464,000 bearers: Mali 265,431, Côte d'Ivoire 96,057, Guinea 51,571, Burkina Faso 36,913, Senegal 2,775, Togo 525, Ghana 416, and 5,416 in India, where the page transcribes the spelling in Marathi. Cited for the distribution and to flag the Indian homonym, not as evidence of ethnic origin.

sources.title: Identités et relations de plaisanterie chez les Peuls de l'ouest du Burkina Faso
sources.notes: Youssouf Diallo, Cahiers d'études africaines, vol. 46, no. 184, 2006, pp. 779–794 (DOI 10.4000/etudesafricaines.15399). Peer-reviewed journal; the author was then affiliated with the Max-Planck-Institut für ethnologische Forschung. The article places Sangaré among the four main Fula clans (Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé, Sangaré) and describes the Sidibé/Sangaré pair as counterparts within the mythical core of Fula identity, maintaining joking relations (dendiraagu) as such; the fieldwork concerns the Fula of western Burkina Faso, which attests the name in that country.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names in the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011–2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89–110. Complete file consulted. The entry Sàngare gives the variant Sankare, links it to the Fula, to Wassoulou and to the Malinké, gives the equivalents Bari, Si and Ba, the joking partners Sidibé and the blacksmiths (nùmu), and the joking nickname Kàngare; it gives no meaning for the name. The entries Bagayogo, Dansoko, Janka and So also name Sangaré among their joking partners, and the entry Bari gives it as an equivalent. The notes of the entry are written in Russian and translated here by us.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, no. 38, 2002, pp. 175–197. Fieldwork in Mali. It sets out what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — applied in varying ways today, it notes — and mutual aid is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair of this fiche, which the entries cited alongside it carry.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, no. 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship eases conflict is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified; the last page is not.

sources.title: Autoportrait du Mali — Les Obstacles à la Paix
sources.notes: Action-research report by the Institut malien de recherche action pour la paix with Interpeace, in partnership with the United Nations, March 2015. Its chapter on sociocultural diversity gives, for each major group in Mali, a few family names followed by "etc.": the list is illustrative, with no method of compilation or source stated. It attests that a name is borne within a group, not where it comes from.

sources.title: Études synchroniques des ethnies et des langues au Mali
sources.notes: Salif Sy, ARLAP research blog (Hypotheses.org), 18 February 2015. Post by a doctoral student in African languages, without peer review, which lists Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré among the names identified as Fula in Mali. Cited to attest the name in this group and in this country, not for its origin.

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, read by V. Vydrin. Entry Jàlo, p. 53: the narrative of the griot Babou Condé of Fadama, collected in 2017, which makes the four names the children of a single Fula mother (the thesis assigns a role to Sidibé twice, keeper of wealth and then warrior, and none to Diallo: we take up only the unambiguous roles), and the ancestry of the four names given by Souleymane Kanté's N'Ko work, in its 2004 edition. Entry Sàngare, p. 120: the variant Sankare, the equivalents Bari, Si and Ba, and the joking nickname Kàngare, with no meaning given for the name. Kanté's original N'Ko text was not read; only its Russian translation was. A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies it transmits.

gaps.reason: A widely known contemporary bearer of this name is well documented by the press and by research, but no statement of her own on her lineage origin has been found; in the absence of such a statement in her own words, no living bearer is named here.
